points.t: You need to describe a rash in notes, a referral, an advice-and-guidance request or a photo request.
The level of the skin involved (epidermis, dermis, subcutis) decides what you see and feel.
Describe lesion type → colour → surface → configuration → distribution, then build the differential from that description.
Non-blanching purpura, blisters or erosions with mucosal involvement, and any changing pigmented lesion.

points: **Macule/patch:** change only in pigment or vascularity without thickening — more/less melanin (freckle, lentigo, café-au-lait; vitiligo) or vascular change (erythema, port-wine stain).
**Papule/plaque:** epidermal thickening (acanthosis, hyperkeratosis) and/or dermal inflammatory infiltrate (psoriasis, lichen planus, eczema) or cellular proliferation.
**Nodule:** deeper dermal/subcutaneous infiltrate, proliferation or deposit (tumour, granuloma, prurigo).
**Wheal:** mast-cell degranulation (histamine) → transient vasodilation and leaky superficial dermal capillaries → dermal oedema without epidermal change (hence no scale, resolves without mark).
**Cyst:** epithelial-lined cavity, e.g. epidermoid cyst from infundibular epithelium producing keratin.
**Scale:** accelerated epidermal turnover (psoriasis — keratinocytes reach the surface in days and retain nuclei = parakeratosis) or abnormal desquamation (ichthyosis, eczema, tinea).

Age pattern: infants — face/cheeks, scalp, extensors (napkin often spared); children — **flexures** (antecubital/popliteal fossae, wrists, ankles, neck); adults — flexures, hands, face/neck, generalised.
Chronic phase: lichenification, excoriations, xerosis, fissures, PIH/hypopigmentation; acute phase: erythema, papulovesicles, weeping, crust.
Sleep disturbance = marker of severity and impact (POEM, CDLQI).

items.name: Macule
items.t: Freckles (ephelides); lentigo; flat drug-eruption/viral exanthem macules
items.where: Close eyes and run a finger over it — no change

items.name: Patch
items.t: Vitiligo; café-au-lait patch; solar lentigo; pityriasis versicolor

items.name: Papule
items.t: Lichen planus (flat-topped, polygonal, purple); molluscum contagiosum (umbilicated); acne papules; viral warts
items.where: Look at the top: flat, dome, umbilicated, scaly, warty

items.name: Plaque
items.t: Chronic plaque psoriasis; discoid (nummular) eczema; tinea corporis; mycosis fungoides (rare, persistent)

items.name: Nodule
items.t: Nodular basal cell carcinoma; nodular prurigo; dermatofibroma; nodular melanoma/SCC; erythema nodosum
items.where: Firm, persistent, growing, bleeding nodule → think malignancy

items.name: Vesicle
items.t: Herpes simplex/eczema herpeticum; varicella/zoster; pompholyx; acute contact dermatitis
items.where: Grouped vesicles on red base = herpes until proven otherwise

items.name: Bulla
items.t: Bullous pemphigoid (tense); bullous impetigo; burns/friction blister; pemphigus (flaccid, rapidly erode); bullous drug reaction
items.where: Tense vs flaccid tells you the split level

items.name: Pustule
items.t: Bacterial folliculitis; acne vulgaris; palmoplantar pustulosis / pustular psoriasis (sterile); rosacea
items.where: A pustule is not automatically infection

items.name: Wheal
items.t: Urticaria (spontaneous/inducible); angio-oedema overlap; insect bites (papular urticaria); dermographism
items.where: Ask: do individual lesions last <24 h and leave no mark?

items.name: Cyst
items.t: Epidermoid cyst (central punctum); pilar (trichilemmal) cyst on scalp; acne cysts; milia (tiny keratin cysts)

points: Inspect in good light with magnification; palpate (wear gloves where appropriate).
Decide **flat vs raised vs fluid-filled vs pus-filled vs deep**; then measure (ruler/photo with scale) to choose the correct size-based term.
Use **diascopy** (press a glass slide): blanching = erythema/vascular dilation; non-blanching = purpura.
Document primary lesion first, then the secondary change (e.g. "erythematous plaques with silvery scale").
Describe in order: **primary lesion + secondary change** (e.g. "lichenified, excoriated plaques in both antecubital fossae").
Gently lift scale/crust — bleeding points under psoriatic scale (Auspitz sign; not routinely elicited).

Assess ulcer: site, size, edge (sloping = venous; punched-out = arterial/neuropathic; rolled = BCC; undermined violaceous = pyoderma), base, exudate, surrounding skin, pulses/ABPI (per local wound pathway).
Atrophy: shiny, wrinkled "cigarette-paper" surface, visible vessels; ask about steroid use, potency, duration.

cards.name: Macule vs patch
cards.clue: Size (<1 cm vs >1 cm) — both flat

cards.name: Papule vs nodule
cards.clue: Size and depth; nodules are deeper/firmer

cards.name: Plaque vs patch
cards.clue: Plaque is palpable (thickened); patch is flat

cards.name: Pustule vs vesicle
cards.clue: Contents: yellow/white pus vs clear fluid (vesicles may become pustular with time)

cards.name: Wheal vs plaque
cards.clue: Wheals are transient (<24 h), shifting, no surface change

cards.name: Cyst vs nodule/lipoma
cards.clue: Punctum, fluctuance, epithelial lining; lipoma is soft, rubbery, no punctum

cards.name: Erosion vs ulcer
cards.clue: Depth — erosion is epidermal only (no scar); ulcer reaches dermis (scar)

cards.name: Scale vs crust
cards.clue: Scale = keratin flakes (white/silver/yellow); crust = dried exudate (honey, brown, haemorrhagic)

cards.name: Lichenification vs plaque
cards.clue: Lichenification = secondary thickening with exaggerated skin lines from rubbing; plaque is the primary raised lesion

cards.name: Lichenification vs PIH
cards.clue: Both often coexist in skin of colour; PIH is colour only (flat), lichenification is palpable thickening

cards.name: Excoriation vs fissure
cards.clue: Excoriation = linear scratch marks (patient-made); fissure = crack from dryness/tension

cards.name: Hypertrophic scar vs keloid
cards.clue: Keloid extends beyond wound and rarely regresses; hypertrophic stays within and may improve

cards.name: Atrophy vs atrophic scar
cards.clue: Atrophy can be reversible (steroid epidermal thinning early); scars are permanent dermal repair

items.t: **Non-blanching** spots or purpura in an unwell patient: think meningococcal sepsis or vasculitis and escalate the same day.
Blisters or erosions with **mouth, eye or genital** involvement: SJS/TEN or immunobullous disease.
Punched-out erosions on eczema: **eczema herpeticum**, same-day assessment.
A **new or changing pigmented lesion**: refer on the suspected-cancer pathway (NICE NG12).

pearls.t: Write the description **before** you write the diagnosis — it protects against anchoring.
Use plain language with patients ("small raised spots", "flat brown mark") but precise terms in notes and referrals.
In skin of colour, erythema may look violaceous, grey, dark brown or be subtle — rely more on texture, warmth and palpation.
Secondary changes tell you **chronicity**: lichenification and atrophy take weeks–months to develop and to reverse — set expectations.
Crust or weeping on eczema = think infection (bacterial **or** herpetic). Punched-out erosions/monomorphic vesicles = eczema herpeticum → urgent same-day review.
Explain atrophy risk honestly but avoid "steroid phobia": under-treatment drives lichenification.
Ask "where did it start and how did it spread?" Geometric or "outside-in" shapes suggest something external. Bilateral symmetrical = more likely endogenous.

Show the family the **difference between lichenification and PIH**: thick skin should soften with adequate steroid + emollient over weeks; pigment change takes months and is not a sign of steroid damage.
